pedagogy.summary: At 6-7 tool choice moves from purely concrete objects to REPRESENTATIONS — number line, hundred square, ruler, part-whole model — and the strategic act becomes matching the representation to the problem's PURPOSE and to the size of the numbers. A jump-counting addition suits a number line; a place-value addition suits a hundred square; a length problem needs a ruler. As numbers grow past ten, counting single cubes in ones becomes slow and error-prone, so a key lesson is trading the concrete tool for a representation that carries the tens. Press children to explain why one representation beats another for a given problem.
bestPractices: Sort problems by 'what are we trying to find?' and match the tool to that purpose (measure → ruler; jump-add → number line) before choosing numbers (EEF: clear rationale)
Show number lines explicitly — EEF finds them a particularly effective representation across KS2/3 — modelling jumps of ten rather than counting marks in ones
Compare two representations for the same problem and discuss 'which helped more and why', which EEF finds develops conceptual understanding
Make the inefficiency of counting big numbers in ones felt, so children choose a representation for efficiency, not just because it is allowed
Keep naming each tool's limitation (a number line doesn't measure a real object; cubes are unwieldy past twenty) so choice stays a fit judgement
keyRepresentations: Number line (jump in tens and ones)
Hundred square (place-value moves — down a row = +10)
commonMisconceptions: Persists with counting single cubes in ones for two-digit numbers (34+28), which is slow and error-prone (EEF: over-reliance on concrete)
Mismatches the tool to the problem's purpose — e.g. reaches for a number line for a 'how long is it?' measuring task instead of a ruler
Draws a number line but counts every mark in ones anyway, using it as a ritual rather than to jump in tens (EEF: answer, not structure)
Thinks a representation is 'babyish' or 'proper' rather than fit-for-purpose, so choice is about status not the problem

learn.summary: For 6-7 year-olds, strategic tool choice shifts from concrete objects to REPRESENTATIONS (number line, hundred square, ruler, part-whole model), and the skill becomes matching the representation to the problem's PURPOSE and to the size of the numbers. As numbers grow past ten, counting single cubes in ones becomes slow and error-prone, so a key lesson is trading the concrete tool for a representation that carries the tens. The central proposed activity gives a child the same chooser facing two problems — a two-digit addition (34+28) where a number line's tens-and-ones jumps are genuinely quicker than counting a cube pile, and a measuring task where a ruler (or a metre stick for a large object), not a number line, fits — then invites them to justify why each tool fits its problem. Alternatives (a convince-a-partner dialogue, a primer comparison board) are intended to serve different pedagogical purposes.

activities.title: Pick the tool, work the problem, justify the fit
feedback: If the child builds 34+28 from single cubes and miscounts, or insists cubes are the way even for big numbers: contrast directly with a +20-then-+8 number-line jump, showing how the representation holds the tens so the ones needn't be counted. Revisit place-value adding strategies.

If the child grabs a number line for the measuring task: sort the two problems by 'what are we trying to find?' and match each tool's purpose; name what a ruler or metre stick does that a number line cannot here.

If the child reaches for a short ruler to measure the door: ask which measuring tool matches the size of the object, prompting the metre stick, so size as well as purpose drives the choice. Revisit measuring with length units.

If the child draws a number line but counts every mark in ones: model the +10 jump and ask 'can you get there in fewer jumps?', linking the tool to place-value structure rather than to the ritual of having drawn it.
Praise specifically when the child names both the efficiency gain (fewer jumps, no miscounting) and a case where the rejected tool would still win.
activities.rationale: A 2D surface with a tool palette lets the child actually pick, use, and feel the efficiency difference between a slow cube pile and a two-jump number line, then justify the choice. The same-child, two-problems contrast is intended to make the strategy concrete rather than a stated rule, though this specific activity is a research-informed proposal, not a separately validated intervention. Number lines modelling jumps of ten, and comparing two representations of the same idea, are highlighted in the EEF guidance.
sourceClaims: Manipulatives and representations must be used purposefully with a clear rationale and to reveal structure not just get an answer; number lines are a particularly effective representation, and comparing different representations of an idea develops conceptual understanding
Proficient students make sound decisions about when a tool is helpful, recognising the insight it gives and its limitations
learnerActions: Solve 34 + 28 using a palette of tools: cubes/base-ten, a number line, a hundred square, a ruler.
If you reach for single cubes, build and count 62 in ones — notice it is slow and easy to miscount. (Base-ten rods group the tens, so they avoid most of this counting.)
On the number line, jump 34 → +20 → 54 → +8 → 62 in two jumps.
On the hundred square (numbered with 1 at the top), add the 20 by moving two rows down to 54, then add 8 by moving forward eight squares (crossing into the next row) to reach 62.
After solving, answer: 'Why did that tool help?' and 'When would cubes actually be the better choice?'

Then tackle a measuring task: 'How long is the ribbon?' (a ruler fits, the number line does not) and 'How tall is the door?' (a metre stick fits better than a short ruler). Explain why the tool follows the problem's purpose AND the size of the object.
activities.intendedInsight: The right tool follows the PURPOSE of the problem and the size of the numbers or object, not habit: a representation that carries the tens (number line, hundred square) spares you counting ones, while a length problem needs a measuring tool matched to the object's size. Cubes remain a good fit for small numbers — this is a fit judgement, not a ranking of tools as 'babyish' or 'proper'.

activities.title: Convince a partner who defaults to cubes
feedback: If the child only says the number line is 'quicker' but cannot name when cubes would be better, prompt: 'Give me a problem where cubes really would be the BEST choice.'
If the child dismisses cubes outright as 'babyish', redirect to fit: cubes are fine, even best, for small numbers — the issue is efficiency with large numbers.
Affirm when the child both defends the efficient tool and identifies a genuine case for cubes.
activities.rationale: A dialogue partner who must be convinced can surface the fit-and-efficiency reasoning aloud and expose whether the child's reason is fit-based or status-based. This is intended as a complementary purpose to the hands-on palette: it targets articulation and justification rather than doing. It is a proposal, not a validated intervention.
sourceClaims: Proficient students make sound decisions about when a tool is helpful, recognising the insight it gives and its limitations
learnerActions: Work with a partner (or in-role character) who always reaches for cubes, even for 34 + 28.
Argue why a number line or hundred square is more efficient for big numbers — point to jumping the tens and avoiding miscounts.
Concede honestly where cubes still win: give a problem (e.g. a small total like 3 + 4) where cubes really would be the best choice.
Answer a probe such as 'What can a hundred square show you that a number line doesn't when you add 28?'
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to explain why one representation beats another for a given problem — and when the rejected tool would in fact be right — is what separates a real fit judgement from a blanket ranking of tools.

activities.title: Primer: what each tool is for
feedback: If the child treats the board as the whole lesson, move them promptly to actually working a problem with a chosen tool — naming purposes is only a warm-up and does not by itself show they can choose and use a tool when solving.
activities.rationale: A static annotated comparison can prime awareness of each tool's purpose and lets the child compare representations, but on its own it does not let the child act, feel the inefficiency, or justify a choice; keep it as a brief primer before the hands-on activity.
sourceClaims: Manipulatives and representations must be used purposefully with a clear rationale and to reveal structure not just get an answer; number lines are a particularly effective representation, and comparing different representations of an idea develops conceptual understanding
learnerActions: Explore a comparison board for number line vs hundred square vs ruler, revealing 'best for…' and 'not for…' notes for each.
Before the main task, predict which tool you would reach for in an addition and in a measuring problem.
activities.intendedInsight: Each representation has a purpose and a limitation — a number line jumps along a count but does not measure a real object; cubes become unwieldy past twenty — so a warm-up can prime 'what each is for'.

constraints: Choose numbers large enough that counting in ones is genuinely inefficient (e.g. 34+28), so the efficiency case for a tens-carrying representation is real rather than asserted.

Frame tool choice as a fit judgement tied to the problem's purpose and number/object size — not as some tools being 'babyish' or 'proper'. Always include a case where the rejected tool (cubes for small numbers) is the better fit.
A comparison/primer board naming 'what each tool is for' is a warm-up: it does not elicit the child working a problem or justifying efficiency, so do not treat it as the main activity.

A single matching/recognition item can ask 'which tool?' but cannot observe the child using the tool or justifying fit and efficiency; recognition-only responses do not elicit independent construction of a strategy.
Keep naming each tool's limitation (a number line doesn't measure a real object; cubes are unwieldy past twenty) so the choice stays a fit judgement.

Include at least one measuring task, and vary the object's size (e.g. ribbon vs door) so the child experiences matching a measuring tool — ruler vs metre stick — to the object, and that a number line does not fit a length problem.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and efficacy wording has been kept qualified accordingly.

The legacy row claimed '3D adds no purchase on tool-fit here' and that a quiz 'cannot observe the child... the WHY is invisible'. These are catalog-fit opinions, not established findings. Retained only the narrowly objective point that recognition-only items do not elicit independent construction; dropped the universal dismissals.

The legacy 'possible'/'poor' fit rankings and product-format vocabulary were removed; the underlying distinct pedagogical purposes (dialogue for justification, primer for priming) were preserved as separate activities.

Arithmetic check: 34 + 28 = 62, and 34 → +20 → 54 → +8 → 62 is correct; on the hundred square +20 is two rows down to 54 and +8 moves forward eight squares (crossing a row boundary) to 62. No arithmetic errors found.
The part-whole model is listed among the topic's tools but is not exercised in any activity, matching the original recommended task; it could optionally be added to the palette.

probeDeeper: Can you give me a problem where cubes really would be the BEST choice?
Show me the fewest jumps you can do on the number line for 34 + 28 — why fewer jumps?
If the problem was 'how tall is the door', which would you pick — number line, ruler, or metre stick — and why?
What can a hundred square show you that a number line doesn't, when you add 28?
assess.correctAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for the child recognising that counting single cubes for numbers this big is slow and error-prone (a limitation), that the number line lets you jump in tens and ones (efficiency and structure), AND that cubes are fine for small numbers — a fit judgement, not 'cubes are babyish'.

errorPatterns.pattern: Persists with counting single cubes in ones for two-digit numbers — slow, error-prone — rather than a representation that carries the tens
errorPatterns.nextMove: Contrast directly with a +20-then-+8 number-line jump; show how the representation holds the tens so ones needn't be counted. Reteach place-value adding strategies.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Builds 34+28 from single cubes and miscounts, or insists cubes are the way even for big numbers

errorPatterns.pattern: Mismatches the tool to the problem's purpose — grabs a number line for a 'how long is it?' measuring task instead of a ruler
errorPatterns.nextMove: Sort problems by 'what are we trying to find?' then match the tool's purpose; name what a ruler does that a number line cannot here. Reteach measuring with length units.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Chooses the wrong class of tool for what the problem asks to find

errorPatterns.pattern: Draws a number line but counts every mark in ones anyway, using it as a ritual rather than to jump in tens
errorPatterns.nextMove: Model the +10 jump and ask 'can you get there in fewer jumps?'; link the tool to place-value structure, not just to having drawn it.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Number line present but every step is a single mark, no tens jumps

responseLevels.gap: Reaches for one tool by habit (usually cubes) or mismatches the tool to the problem's purpose, with no efficiency or fit reasoning.
responseLevels.full: Unprompted, matches the tool to the problem's purpose and the size of the numbers, justifies by efficiency and structure (jump the tens), names when the rejected tool would in fact be the right choice, and picks a ruler for a measuring task.
responseLevels.partial: Chooses a reasonable representation and, when prompted, says the number line is 'quicker', but cannot say when cubes would be better or slips back into counting marks in ones.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: To work out 34 + 28, one child got out 62 cubes and counted them one by one; another used a number line and jumped +20 then +8. Which was the better tool for these numbers, and why? And when WOULD cubes be the better choice?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: 34+28 is big enough that counting cubes in ones is genuinely inefficient, so a strategic chooser points to efficiency and place-value jumps; a non-strategic child either counts everything or dismisses cubes outright with no fit reason. The 'when would cubes be better?' turn separates a real fit judgement from a blanket ranking of tools.
